corrected_value.title: Social identity contingencies: how diversity cues signal threat or safety for African Americans in mainstream institutions

decision.location: Primary Project Report 97 (https://osf.io/download/3rxvs/), Introduction & Method, source_view.json lines 1048-1049; Confirmatory Analyses & References, lines 1055-1057; Master CSV (https://osf.io/download/fgjvw/) Study Num 97, lines 1162-1163; Appendix Table, p. 38, line 68
decision.quote: Replication of “Social identity contingencies: How diversity cues signal threat or safety for African Americans in mainstream institutions” by V Purdie-Vaughns, CM Steele, PG Davies, R Ditlmann, JR Crosby (2008, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology). Kathleen Schmidt kes7z@virginia.edu Introduction In their original paper “Social identity contingencies: How diversity cues signal threat or safety for African Americans in mainstream institutions,” Purdie-Vaughns, Steele, Davies, Ditlmann, and Crosby (2008) suggest that people belonging to a group that is vulnerable to prejudice are especially sensitive to social identity contingencies—the set of potential “judgments, stereotypes, opportunities, restrictions, and treatments” related to social identity in an environment (Purdie-Vaughns et al. 2008). The researchers suggest that a given setting can produce expectations about social contingencies that affect personal comfort in that setting. In this replication of Purdie-Vaughns et al. (2008), I sought to reproduce the methodology used in the original paper as exactly as possible.
decision.reason: 1. Empirical retesting: In Primary Project Report 97 (https://osf.io/download/3rxvs/, lines 1048-1057) and Master CSV Study Num 97 (lines 1162-1163), replicator Kathleen Schmidt collected new empirical data on Amazon Mechanical Turk (final analyzed N = 1,490 African American and White adults) to replicate Experiment 3 of Purdie-Vaughns et al. (2008), testing the 2 (participant race: African American or White) x 2 (fairness cue: high or low) between-subjects ANOVA interaction on institutional trust in a setting with low minority representation and a colorblind philosophy. Whereas the original study reported a significant interaction, F(1, 73) = 12.19, p = .001, partial eta^2 = .1431 (N = 90), the replication found a non-significant interaction in the opposite direction, F(1, 1486) = 2.03, p = .154, partial eta^2 = .001 (Note: the blind coder listed study_numbers as '2' from the Master CSV 'Replicated study number (R)' column, whereas the primary report narrative on line 1048 explicitly specifies 'this study is a replication of Experiment 3'). 2. Original work identity: The source explicitly cites 'Purdie-Vaughns, V., Steele, C. M., Davies, P. G., Ditlmann, R., & Crosby, J. R. (2008). Social identity contingencies: how diversity cues signal threat or safety for African Americans in mainstream institutions. Journal of personality and social psychology, 94(4), 615' (line 1057; Master CSV pages 615-30, line 1162). No original article DOI is printed in the source text (the OSF DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/2R7NK on p. 38 is for the replication project), so doi is omitted. 3. Absence from shipped rows: All 93 supplied shipped rows for 10.1126/science.aac4716 were inspected; none represents Purdie-Vaughns et al. (2008, JPSP, 94(4), 615-630). Shipped rows sharing co-authors—row 1625 (Goff, Steele, & Davies, 2008, JPSP, 94(1), 91, 'The space between us: Stereotype threat and distance in interracial contexts', replicated in Report 81 / Study Num 87) and row 1907 (Crosby, Monin, & Richardson, 2008, Psychological Science, 19(3), 226, 'Where Do We Look During Potentially Offensive Behavior?', replicated in Report 48 / Study Num 132)—are distinct original articles with different designs and replication reports. 4. corrected_value.title: Anchor precision influences the amount of adjustment

decision.location: Primary Project Report 10 (https://osf.io/download/ehjdm/), Results, Discussion & Reference, source_view.json line 222; Master CSV (https://osf.io/download/fgjvw/) Study Num 111, lines 1172-1173; Appendix Table, p. 37, line 66
decision.quote: Confirmatory analysis A 2 X 2 ANOVA revealed a main effect of motivation, F(1,116) = 71.06, p < .001, = .38, indicating that people told to adjust by a large amount adjusted more (M = .27, SD = .39) than people told to adjust by a small amount (M = -.27, SD = .32). There was also a main effect of anchor precision, F(1,116) = 6.28, p = .014, = .05, indicating that people given the round anchor adjusted more (M = .08, SD = .48) than people given the precise anchor (M = -.08, SD = .40). There was no interaction between motivation and precision, F < 1. Discussion Summary of Replication Attempt These findings represent a partial replication of Janiszewski and Uy (2008). The central claim of their paper – that anchor precision influences the degree of adjustment was supported. Additionally, these data replicated the main effect of motivation observed in their study. There was no evidence of the reported interaction.
decision.reason: 1. Empirical retesting: In Primary Project Report 10 (https://osf.io/download/ehjdm/, lines 219-222) and Master CSV Study Num 111 (lines 1172-1173), replicator Jesse Chandler collected new data from 126 undergraduate participants (N = 120 analyzed after excluding 6 who discussed answers) to replicate Study 4a of Janiszewski and Uy (2008) (report heading says 'Replication of Study 4b', while the body text on line 219 states 'Study 4a was selected for replication (rather than 4b)'). Using a 2 (anchor precision: round vs. precise) x 2 (motivation to adjust: small vs. large) ANOVA on standardized price-estimate adjustments, the replication reproduced the focal main effect of anchor precision, F(1, 116) = 6.28, p = .014, partial eta^2 = .05 (original F(1, 55) = 6.88, p_rep = .947, eta^2 = .02, N = 59) and the main effect of motivation, F(1, 116) = 71.06, p < .001, partial eta^2 = .38 (original F(1, 55) = 89.20, p_rep = .99, eta^2 = .60), but found no interaction, F < 1 (original F(1, 55) = 3.55, p_rep = .86). 2. Original work identity: The report reference (line 222) explicitly cites 'Janiszewski, C., D. Uy. 2008. Anchor precision influences the amount of adjustment. Psychological Science, 19,121–127.' (also listed in the Master CSV line 1172 as 'Precision of the anchor influences the amount of adjustment.,"C Janiszewski, D Uy",PS,19,2,121-7'). No original article DOI is printed in the source text, so doi is omitted. 3. corrected_value.title: Preschoolers' perspective taking in word learning: do they blindly follow eye gaze?

decision.location: Primary Project Report 27 (https://osf.io/download/ictp5/), Confirmatory analysis & Discussion, source_view.json lines 366-367; Master CSV (https://osf.io/download/fgjvw/) Study Num 115, lines 1175-1176; Appendix Table, p. 38, line 67
decision.quote: Confirmatory analysis The data from 20 participants were analyzed in order to attempt to replicate the original authors’ primary finding that older children performed at above-chance levels on “where” trials, answering an average of 1.41 out of 2 trials correctly, t(31) = 3.23, prep = .97. In our replication study, a one-sample t-test showed no such trend, M = 0.625, t(7) = -1.426, p = .197. Younger children (M = .833) also did not perform at above-chance levels on “where” trials, t(11) = -.804, p = .438. Similarly, neither the older (M = 1.125) or younger (M = 1.08) group performed at above-chance levels on “there” trials, t(7) = .357, p = .732 and t(11) = .364, p = .723, respectively. At one point during the planning of this replication, independent measures t-tests comparing younger versus older students on the number of correct “where” trial and “there” trial responses had been identified as the key finding. These analyses also showed no differences between younger and older children on “where” trials, t(18) = .627, p = .539, nor on “there” trials, t(18) = -1.04, p = .918. Discussion Summary of Replication Attempt Unlike in Nurmsoo and Bloom (2008), the confirmatory analysis for the current replication attempt did not reveal above-chance performance by older children on “where” trials. Thus, it is clear that we failed to replicate the original study’s finding.
decision.reason: 1. Empirical retesting: In Primary Project Report 27 (https://osf.io/download/ictp5/, lines 363-367) and Master CSV Study Num 115 (lines 1175-1176), Benjamin Brown and colleagues tested N = 20 preschool children (n = 12 younger, ages 25-36 months; n = 8 older, ages 46-54 months) using the original authors' physical screen and novel object stimuli to replicate Study 1 of Nurmsoo and Bloom (2008). Whereas the original study found that older children selected the correct object above chance on 'where' trials, M = 1.41 out of 2, t(31) = 3.23, p_rep = .97, d = .571, the replication one-sample t-test found no above-chance performance in older children, M = 0.625, t(7) = -1.426, p = .197, or younger children, M = .833, t(11) = -.804, p = .438. 2. No original article DOI is printed in the source text, so doi is omitted. 3. corrected_value.title: Errors Are Aversive: Defensive Motivation and the Error-Related Negativity

decision.location: Primary Project Report 34 (https://osf.io/download/82bwv/), Section 4.2 Statistical results, source_view.json lines 451-452; Report header, line 447; Master CSV (https://osf.io/download/fgjvw/) Study Num 120, lines 1180-1181; Appendix Table, p. 38, line 68
decision.quote: 4.2 Statistical results A robust ERN was observed (mean amplitude = 6.44µV; SEM = .73) which was similar in magnitude to the original study (see Figure 1). This difference between ERP amplitudes following errors vs. correct responses was significant (t(40) = 8.69, p < .01). An error potentiated startle response was also apparent (see Figure 2), the magni- tude of which corresponded closely with the original study (mean difference between error and correct trials = 2.44µV; SEM = 1.17). This effect was significant. Paired t tests found that startle magnitude was greater following errors than following either subtype of correct trial, whether predictable, t(40) = 3.51, p < .01, or unpredictable t(28) = 2.08, p < .05. The main finding of the original study, a correlation between ERN and EPS am- plitude, did not reach the threshold for significance in our replication: r = -.25, p = .11, one-tailed. The original study reported a significant correlation: r = -.38, p < .05, one-tailed.
decision.reason: 1. Empirical retesting: In Primary Project Report 34 (https://osf.io/download/82bwv/, lines 447-456) and Master CSV Study Num 120 (lines 1180-1181), replicators Melissa Lewis and Michael Pitts tested 51 subjects (final analyzed N = 43 after impedance/artifact exclusions) in an arrow flanker task with acoustic startle probes, measuring EEG error-related negativity (ERN) and EMG error-potentiated startle (EPS) to replicate Hajcak and Foti (2008). While the replication reproduced the ERN main effect, t(40) = 8.69, p < .01, and EPS main effects for predictable correct trials, t(40) = 3.51, p < .01, and unpredictable correct trials, t(28) = 2.08, p < .05, the focal zero-order correlation between ERN and EPS magnitude did not reach statistical significance, r = -.25, p = .11, one-tailed (N = 43), compared to the original study's r = -.38, p < .05, one-tailed (N = 31). 2. corrected_value.title: The sunny side of fairness: Preference for fairness activates reward circuitry (and disregarding unfairness activates self-control circuitry)

decision.location: Primary Project Report 35 (https://osf.io/download/nxp9w/), Introduction, source_view.json lines 456-458; Overview of the Results & Neural Results, lines 461-464; Master CSV (https://osf.io/download/fgjvw/) Study Num 121, lines 1181-1182; Appendix Table, p. 38, line 68
decision.quote: Replication of “The sunny side of fairness: Preference for fairness activates reward circuitry (and disregarding unfairness activates self-control circuitry)” by G Tabibnia, AB Satpute, MD Lieberman (2008, Psychological Science) Anastasia Rigney Taru Flagan Jennifer Beer beerutexas@gmail.com Introduction In their original paper “The sunny side of fairness: Preference for fairness activates reward circuitry (and disregarding unfairness activates self-control circuitry,” Tabibnia, Satpute, and Lieberman (2008) discuss the difficulties in separating the desire for fairness from the desire for material gain in the context of economic decision making. Accordingly, there had been little research on whether fair proposals produce positive emotional response due to its inherent fairness regardless of material gain. The original authors suggest that ultimatum games that require bilateral bargaining allow these motives to be tested independently. In this replication of Tabibnia et al. (2008), we sought to reproduce the methodology used in the original paper. The present work was conducted as part of the Reproducibility Project: Psychology which asks volunteers to replicate the final study in their chosen paper. Therefore, this is a direct replication of Experiment 2.
decision.reason: 1. Empirical retesting: In Primary Project Report 35 (https://osf.io/download/nxp9w/, lines 456-464) and Master CSV Study Num 121 (lines 1181-1182), Anastasia Rigney, Taru Flagan, and Jennifer Beer conducted an fMRI replication (N = 24 analyzed out of 25 scanned on a 3T Siemens Skyra) of Experiment 2 of Tabibnia, Satpute, and Lieberman (2008). The replication reproduced the behavioral pattern of offer acceptance (higher acceptance for fair vs. unfair offers) and the focal neural findings: fair > unfair offers activated reward regions in the dorsal striatum (z = 3.23) and orbitofrontal cortex (z = 2.81 right, z = 3.84 left), and accepting subjectively unfair offers > baseline activated the left VLPFC (z = 4.92, p_rep > 0.99) and right LPFC extending to VLPFC (z = 5.43, p_rep > 0.99, d = 2.22), replicating the original right VLPFC activation (t(11) = 5.39, p_rep > 0.99, d = 3.25, N = 12), while auxiliary insula analyses (Planned analyses 3-5) did not replicate in the original direction. 2. Original work identity: Report 35 (line 456) and Master CSV Study Num 121 (lines 1181-1182) explicitly identify the original paper as 'The sunny side of fairness: Preference for fairness activates reward circuitry (and disregarding unfairness activates self-control circuitry)' by G Tabibnia, AB Satpute, MD Lieberman (2008, Psychological Science, 19(4), 339-347). No original article DOI is printed in the source text, so doi is omitted. 3.
